title: Chemical characterization and mercury speciation in six species of wild edible mushrooms – assessment of mercury exposure
content: Wild edible mushrooms can accumulate mercury (Hg) even in uncontaminated environments, posing health risks to consumers. In the present study, six edible mushroom species from the Western Carpathians, Romania – Boletus edulis, Boletus pinophilus, Russula cyanoxantha, Russula virescens, Cantharellus cibarius, and Amanita rubescens – were analysed for proximate composition and metal content, focusing on total Hg and methylmercury (MeHg). The impact of mercury speciation on potential consumer health risks was also assessed. The speciation analysis employed a non-chromatographic technique involving double liquid–liquid extraction, with subsequent quantification conducted using thermal decomposition atomic absorption spectrometry (TD-AAS). Soil Hg concentrations were determined by TD-AAS, and bioconcentration factors were computed as ratios of mushroom-to-soil Hg concentrations. Although proximate composition varied among species, the distribution of components was consistent, following the trend: carbohydrates > proteins > ash > lipids. The carbohydrate content ranged from 59.1 to 69.8 g/100 g dry mass (dm), the protein content from 21.5 g/100 g to 28.6 g/100 g, the ash content from 5.2 to 8.3 g/100 g, while the lipid content from 1.6 to 6.0 g/100 g. Among the mineral elements, K, P, and S, were present at the highest concentrations, with average values (g kg−1 dm) decreasing in the order K (25.9) >> P (5.49) > S (2.74). The average contents (mg kg−1 dm) of the other mineral elements generally decreased in the order Na (755) ≈ Mg (748) > Ca (552) > Zn (131) ≈ Fe (110) >> Cu (40.1) > Mn (16.0) > Cr (2.19) > Hg (1.63) > Ni (1.43) ≈ Pb (1.18) > Cd (0.19). The total Hg ranged from 0.12 to 3.5 mg kg−1 dry mass across species, while MeHg accounted for 1.0–12.7% of the total. All of the studied species had soil-to-mushroom bioconcentration factors over 1, while Boletus spp. exceeded 20. Moderate consumption of the analysed edible mushrooms does not pose a risk from total Hg or MeHg content. However, it is advisable to limit consumption to less than 1000 g (wet weight) per week, particularly regarding B. edulis and B. pinophilus.
